html:
Rooibos, Afrikaans for "red bush", is a shrub of the Cederberg mountains north of Cape Town, whose leaves make a caffeine-free red tea. Long brewed by local Khoisan people, it was first farmed in the 1930s and is now drunk around the world.

The plant grows only in a small part of South Africa's fynbos country, in sandy soils and a winter-rain climate. Khoekhoe and San people cut the wild bushes, bruised the leaves and let them ferment, which turns them red. Settlers took up the drink, and in the early 20th century traders began selling it more widely.

In the 1930s a local doctor, Pieter le Fras Nortier, worked out with farmers how to germinate and grow it, and plantations followed. Rooibos became a cheap substitute when imported tea was short during the Second World War.

From the 1990s it spread abroad as a health drink. In 2021 the European Union gave it protected status: only rooibos grown in the Cederberg region of South Africa can carry the name.
